ⓘ Notes
The relationship map and glossary of all the parts, plus your learning progress, quiz scores and entry points to every lab.

Why it’s designed this way: After studying, tying the parts together in one picture is what really “understanding the big picture” means.

On this page:

🔬 Level 3 · detail

🧒 In plain words first

This is one big map of the whole site: from top to bottom, roughly “getting things done with AI → the model → the parts inside it → seeing and hearing → how it is trained → the machines it runs on”. Tap any box to see what it is and jump to the stop that explains it.

App overview
The user’s sentenceWhere the whole system starts: saying what you want in plain words.App overview—
Agent app layerWraps the LLM into a program that “gets things done”: planning, tool calls, memory, loops, permissions.App overview—
LLM (large language model)The agent’s “brain”: reads a passage of text and writes what comes next, one token at a time.App overviewAgent app layer
Multimodal encoders / decodersThe LLM’s “eyes, ears and paintbrush”: turning images and sounds into tokens, or tokens back into images and sounds.App overviewLLM (large language model)
Training systemWhere the model’s skills come from: pretraining → instruction tuning → preference alignment → reasoning RL.App overviewLLM (large language model)
Compute and servingMakes the model actually run: GPU clusters, inference serving, KV cache, batching, quantization.App overviewLLM (large language model)
Using agents
Using agents (overview)The same agent (LLM + tools + loop) can be used in many ways; they differ in only four things.Using agentsAgent app layer
Work alongside itYou sit beside it: you see every step, and key steps wait for your OK.Using agentsUsing agents (overview)
Let it run aloneYou hand the task over, it runs to the end in an isolated environment, and you review the result afterwards.Using agentsUsing agents (overview)
Extend itWithout changing the model you can teach it more: add tools, connect MCP servers, install skills.Using agentsUsing agents (overview)
Use it wellWith the same agent, results differ a lot depending on how clearly you brief it and how clean its context is.Using agentsUsing agents (overview)
Using agents › Work alongside it
Chat assistantAsk and answer in a web page or app; the least access, the safest, and the most common use.Work alongside itWork alongside it
Coding agent in the editorLives in your code editor: reads your project, edits files, runs commands, while you review and accept each change.Work alongside itWork alongside it
Command-line coding agentA coding agent in the terminal: reads and writes files, runs commands, uses git; a permission level decides how much it does on its own.Work alongside itWork alongside it
Browser / computer-use agentOperates web pages or a computer like a person: looks at screenshots / the page structure, then clicks, types, scrolls.Work alongside itWork alongside it
Using agents › Let it run alone
Background / cloud agentHand the task to the cloud: it works alone on a copy of the code and hands back a branch or a pull request (PR).Let it run aloneLet it run alone
Routines & automationNo need to ask: on a schedule or when something happens, the agent runs a fixed prompt automatically.Let it run aloneLet it run alone
Multi-agent teamsA coordinator splits a big task, sends parts to several workers in parallel, and a reviewer checks and merges the results.Let it run aloneLet it run alone
Using agents › Extend it
Tools (function calling)A tool = a name + what it is for + a parameter format; the model writes JSON per the manual and the program actually runs it.Extend itExtend it
MCP (Model Context Protocol)An open protocol proposed in late 2024: any AI app can plug in tools and data that others have built, in one standard way.Extend itExtend it
Skills (skill packs)A folder: instructions for “how to do a kind of task” (plus optional scripts and templates); normally only its name and one-line description are shown.Extend itExtend it
Using agents › Use it well
A clear task briefA good brief states four things: the goal, the background, what not to do, and what counts as done.Use it wellUse it well
Managing contextThe context is a workbench of limited size: put on what is relevant, take off what is not.Use it wellUse it well
Model APIs
Model APIs (overview)An API lets your program ask the model for you: send text, get a reply.Model APIsAgent app layer
API keyA string that proves “it is you; bill me”: effectively your wallet.Model APIsModel APIs (overview)
OpenAI-compatible formatMany platforms (and local runners) accept the same request format; the same code moves by changing three things.Model APIsModel APIs (overview)
Paying by tokensBill = input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price, priced per million tokens.Model APIsModel APIs (overview)
Run models locally
Running locally (overview)Download an open-weights model and run it yourself: data stays home, no per-token bill.Run models locallyAgent app layer
Memory estimateMemory while running ≈ parameters × bits ÷ 8 + KV cache + the program.Run models locallyRunning locally (overview)
Local runnersPrograms that run model files: Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM.Run models locallyRunning locally (overview)
Model files and quant levelsIn a file name, 8B, Q4_K_M and .gguf are the size, the quantization level and the format.Run models locallyRunning locally (overview)
Let AI do tasks
Let AI do tasks (overview)Say what the job is, pick a fitting agent, then check what it hands back.Let AI do tasksUsing agents (overview)
Pick an agent by taskFor one job, first decide: should the AI work step by step with you, or take the task and finish it alone?Let AI do tasksLet AI do tasks (overview)
Check its outputWhat the AI hands back is like a classmate’s homework: it counts only after you mark it.Let AI do tasksLet AI do tasks (overview)
Add skills to AI
Add skills to an AI (overview)Choose one of four add-ons by what you want it to gain: a tool, an MCP server, a skill pack or a prompt template.Add skills to AIExtend it
Catalogue of MCP servers and skillsReal MCP servers and skill packs sorted by use, each with its official link.Add skills to AIAdd skills to an AI (overview)
Check access before installingInstalling an MCP server hands the agent a key; first see which doors it opens.Add skills to AIAdd skills to an AI (overview)
Build an agent
Build your own agent (overview)Two roads: drag and drop on a platform (no-code / low-code), or write code (an SDK plus a tool-calling loop).Build an agentAgent app layer
No-code / low-code platformsDrag “nodes” on a web canvas into a flow: model, knowledge base, tools, decisions; no code.Build an agentBuild your own agent (overview)
Build in code (SDK + loop)Send requests with an OpenAI-compatible SDK and write the loop yourself: model asks for a tool → program runs it → result goes back to the model.Build an agentBuild your own agent (overview)
App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Math · Calculus
LimitThe value f(x)f(x)f(x) gets arbitrarily close to as xxx gets close to aaa.Math · Calculus—
DerivativeThe instantaneous rate of change: if the input moves a little, how many times as much the output moves.Math · CalculusLimit
Chain ruleThe derivative of a composition is the product of the layers’ derivatives: (f∘g)′(x)=f′(g(x)) g′(x)(f\circ g)'(x)=f'(g(x))\,g'(x)(f∘g)′(x)=f′(g(x))g′(x).Math · CalculusDerivative
Partial derivatives & gradientWith several inputs, differentiate with respect to each one (holding the rest fixed) and stack the results into a vector ∇f\nabla f∇f.Math · CalculusDerivative
IntegralThe limit of adding up many tiny pieces; geometrically, the area under a curve.Math · CalculusLimit
App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Math · Linear algebra
Vectors & dot productA list of numbers is a vector; the dot product a⋅b=∑iaibia\cdot b=\sum_i a_i b_ia⋅b=∑i​ai​bi​ measures how much two vectors point the same way.Math · Linear algebra—
Matrix multiplication(AB)ij=∑kAikBkj(AB)_{ij}=\sum_k A_{ik}B_{kj}(AB)ij​=∑k​Aik​Bkj​: the dot product of row i with column j.Math · Linear algebraVectors & dot product
Linear maps & determinantA 2×2 matrix turns the unit square into a parallelogram whose area is multiplied by ∣det⁡A∣=∣ad−bc∣|\det A|=|ad-bc|∣detA∣=∣ad−bc∣.Math · Linear algebraMatrix multiplication
Transpose & JacobianThe matrix of all partial derivatives of a vector function, Jij=∂yi/∂xjJ_{ij}=\partial y_i/\partial x_jJij​=∂yi​/∂xj​; gradients flow back through its transpose.Math · Linear algebraMatrix multiplication
App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Math · Probability & information
Distributions & expectationOne probability per outcome, summing to 1; the expectation E[X]=∑xx p(x)\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_x x\,p(x)E[X]=∑x​xp(x) is the probability-weighted average.Math · Probability & information—
Conditional probability & BayesP(A∣B)=P(B∣A) P(A)P(B)P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}P(A∣B)=P(B)P(B∣A)P(A)​: how the probability of A updates after seeing evidence B.Math · Probability & informationDistributions & expectation
SoftmaxTurns any scores zzz into probabilities: pi=ezi/∑jezjp_i=e^{z_i}/\sum_j e^{z_j}pi​=ezi​/∑j​ezj​.Math · Probability & informationDistributions & expectation
Entropy & cross-entropyEntropy H(p)=−∑plog⁡pH(p)=-\sum p\log pH(p)=−∑plogp measures uncertainty; cross-entropy H(p,q)=−∑plog⁡qH(p,q)=-\sum p\log qH(p,q)=−∑plogq measures how badly q predicts p.Math · Probability & informationDistributions & expectation
KL divergenceKL(p∥q)=∑plog⁡pq\mathrm{KL}(p\Vert q)=\sum p\log\frac{p}{q}KL(p∥q)=∑plogqp​: how far apart two distributions are; always ≥ 0, and 0 only when they are equal.Math · Probability & informationEntropy & cross-entropy
App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Math · Optimization
Gradient descentRepeat θ←θ−η ∇L(θ)\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\,\nabla L(\theta)θ←θ−η∇L(θ) to lower the loss step by step.Math · Optimization—
Learning rate & convergenceWith too small a step η\etaη progress is slow; too large and it oscillates or diverges.Math · OptimizationGradient descent
Stochastic gradient (mini-batch)Each step estimates the gradient from a small batch of examples instead of all the data.Math · OptimizationGradient descent
Momentum & AdamMomentum accumulates past gradients; Adam also scales each parameter’s step by the size of its gradients.Math · OptimizationGradient descent
App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics › Math · Derivations & proofs
Backprop derivationApply the chain rule layer by layer backwards; one backward pass gives every parameter’s gradient.Math · Derivations & proofs—
Softmax + CE gradient p − yThe gradient with respect to the scores zzz is “predicted probabilities − correct answer”: ∇zL=p−y\nabla_z L=p-y∇z​L=p−y.Math · Derivations & proofsBackprop derivation
Attention’s √dₖ scalingDividing the scores by dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ brings the dot product’s variance back to 1, so softmax does not saturate.Math · Derivations & proofsBackprop derivation
Gradient through residualsThe Jacobian of y=x+F(x)y=x+F(x)y=x+F(x) is I+∂F/∂xI+\partial F/\partial xI+∂F/∂x, so the gradient always has a straight-through path.Math · Derivations & proofsBackprop derivation
Policy gradient∇θJ=E[R ∇θlog⁡πθ(τ)]\nabla_\theta J=\mathbb{E}\big[R\,\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(\tau)\big]∇θ​J=E[R∇θ​logπθ​(τ)]: raise the probability of outputs that earned high reward.Math · Derivations & proofsBackprop derivation
App overview › Agent › LLM · additions
Reasoning models (think, then answer)Before answering, the model writes a draft-like chain of thought and then the final answer: spending more compute at inference time to get more answers right.LLM—
Hallucination: causes and fixesThe model says something fluent and plausible that is actually wrong or made up.LLM—
In-context learning (few-shot)Without changing any parameters, put a few input→output examples in the prompt and the model follows the pattern on a new task.LLM—
Greedy decoding and beam searchWithout random sampling, how to build a whole sentence from per-step probabilities: take the single best word each step (greedy), or keep several candidates at once (beam search).LLMSampling
PerplexityA common measure of how unsure a language model is about the next word: lower is better.LLMLoss (cross-entropy)
BPE (byte-pair encoding)The most common way to build a tokenizer: start from single characters and keep merging the pair that occurs together most often into a new token until the vocabulary is big enough.LLMTokenizer
App overview › Agent · additions
Structured output and constrained decodingMakes the model’s output follow a format exactly (such as valid JSON) so a program can read it directly.Agent④ Tool call
Embedding recall + rerankingFirst fetch a batch of candidates quickly with embeddings (recall), then reorder them with a finer model (rerank), and finally give the top few to the LLM with their sources.AgentMemory / RAG
A2A: the agent-to-agent protocolLets agents built by different teams and frameworks discover each other, delegate tasks and return results.AgentMulti-agent collaboration
App overview › Training & RL · additions
Distributed parallel trainingSplits one training run over hundreds or thousands of accelerators: split the data, split each layer, split the sequence of layers, split the experts.Training & RLData and compute
Data engineering and synthetic dataTurns raw web pages into training text: extract, deduplicate, filter, mix, and add synthetic data where needed.Training & RLMassive data + next-word guessing
RL training for agentsLets the model act in a real task environment (calling tools, editing code) and rewards it for finishing the task, so it gets better at getting work done.Training & RLReasoning RL (verifiable rewards)
Safety alignment: red-teaming, jailbreaks, constitutional rulesTrains the model itself to refuse harmful requests without over-refusing, and actively hunts for its weak spots.Training & RLPreference alignment (RLHF etc.)
Evaluation and contaminationScores models on fixed question sets to compare them; but scores can be inflated if the model has seen the questions.Training & RLTraining system
Scaling lawsAn empirical rule: as model size, data and compute grow, the loss falls smoothly as a power law, so it can be predicted in advance.Training & RLData and compute
Regularisation: dropout, weight decay, early stoppingStops the model memorising its training data (overfitting) so it also works on data it has not seen.Training & RLBackpropagation + gradient descent
Pooling and the feature hierarchy (CNN)The step in a convolutional network that shrinks a feature map while keeping the strongest signals; stacked up, the network goes from edges to textures, parts and whole objects.Training & RLArchitectures: MLP / CNN / RNN / Transformer
pass@k evaluationA common score for coding problems: let the model try k times; it counts as solved if any attempt passes the tests. pass@k is the chance of that.Training & RLEvaluation and contamination
LR warmup, cosine decay and gradient clippingThree common tools in LLM training: steps that start small, grow, then shrink slowly, and a cap so no single update blows up.Training & RLBackpropagation + gradient descent
Chinchilla scaling formulaA fitted formula: give it the parameter count N and the training tokens D and it estimates the loss after training; add the compute constraint and it tells you how big the model should be for a budget.Training & RLScaling laws
App overview › Multimodal · additions
Real-time voice: cascade vs end-to-end full duplexLets an AI hold a phone-like conversation in real time: listen while speaking, be interrupted, hear tone of voice.MultimodalAudio encoder
Document and screenshot understanding (OCR, layout, tables)Lets a model read invoices, PDFs, tables and screenshots: not just the characters, but which part is a title, a header or a button.MultimodalVision encoder (ViT)
Image editing and video understandingEdits an image from one sentence (“make the sky a sunset”), and understands what is happening in a video.MultimodalImage generation (diffusion)
App overview · additions
Compliance: copyright, privacy, AI-content labellingThe rules for generating and publishing with AI: copyright in training data and outputs, personal-information protection, and labelling AI-generated content.App overviewAgent app layer
ProductsCommon agent products, grouped by the way you use them, each with its official link.App overviewUsing agents (overview)
Neural-net basicsEvery layer inside a Transformer is a neural network: many small “weighted sum + activation” parts stacked in layers.App overview—
Reference & mapThe relationship map and glossary of all the parts, plus your progress and an entry to every lab.App overview—
CalculusLimits → derivatives → chain rule → gradient: the math of “which way to move each parameter”.App overview—
Linear algebraVectors → matrices → determinant → Jacobian: what one “layer” actually computes.App overview—
Probability & informationDistributions → softmax → cross-entropy → KL: how a model expresses uncertainty and how it is scored.App overview—
OptimizationSteepest descent → learning rate → mini-batches → Adam: the math of every training step.App overview—
Derivations & proofsBackprop → p − y → √dₖ → residuals → policy gradient: full derivations of the model’s key formulas.App overview—
App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics · additions
Autoencoders, VAEs and GANsThe prequel to today’s image generators: learn to compress data into a few numbers, or learn to produce samples that look real.Neural Network BasicsNeural network
App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › FFN & output · additions
Interpretability: probes and featuresAnswers “what has the model actually learned inside?” by reading concepts out of the numbers in its middle layers.FFN & outputFilter switch (activation function)
App overview › Agent › LLM › MoE & efficiency · additions
Other architectures: Mamba, hybrids, diffusion LMsSequence models being explored beyond the Transformer: cheaper and faster on long text, or generating in a different way.MoE & efficiencyLong-context techniques
Mixed precision (BF16, FP8) and FlashAttentionTwo low-level tricks that make training and inference faster and lighter on memory: compute with shorter numbers, and move data more cleverly.MoE & efficiencyQuantization
App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention · additions
Rotary position embedding (RoPE)A way to put “which position is this word in” into attention: rotate Q and K by an angle that depends on position.AttentionPosition info
App overview › Agent
Agent loopObserve → think → act (call a tool) → check the result → think again… until done.AgentAgent app layer
① User goalWhere the task begins: the result you want.AgentAgent loop
② Observe / contextAll the text the model can “see” this round.AgentAgent loop
③ Think / decide (LLM)The LLM reads the context and decides: answer directly, or call which tool with which arguments.AgentAgent loop
④ Tool callThe model outputs a structured “call request” (e.g. JSON) that an external program actually executes.AgentAgent app layer
Tool manual (function description)Text that tells the model “which tools exist, what they’re for, and how to fill in the arguments”.Agent④ Tool call
⑤ Tool resultThe return value (or error) after the program runs the tool, appended to the context as text.AgentAgent loop
⑥ Final answerThe model judges the goal achieved and reports in natural language.AgentAgent loop
Planning and task decompositionBreaks a big task into small steps and revises the plan based on results if needed.AgentAgent app layer
Memory / RAGShort-term memory is the context; long-term memory lives outside and is retrieved into the context when needed.AgentAgent app layer
ChunkingSplits long documents into short passages of a few hundred words.AgentMemory / RAG
Vectorization (embedding model)Turns a passage into a list of numbers (a vector); texts with similar meanings get similar vectors.AgentMemory / RAG
Vector databaseA database specialized in storing lots of vectors and quickly finding “the few nearest”.AgentMemory / RAG
Retrieve top-kCompares the question’s vector and puts the k most similar chunks of original text into the context.AgentMemory / RAG
Multi-agent collaborationSeveral agents with different roles pass tasks and results to each other.AgentAgent app layer
OrchestratorSplits the task, assigns the parts, gathers the results.AgentMulti-agent collaboration
WorkerFocuses on completing one subtask, such as research or writing code.AgentMulti-agent collaboration
ReviewerChecks whether the result is correct and complete, and sends it back if not.AgentMulti-agent collaboration
MCP / tool protocolA “universal socket” for tools: the tool provider implements it once and every AI app can connect.Agent④ Tool call
AI app (host)The AI app the user uses directly, containing the LLM-calling logic and the MCP client.AgentMCP / tool protocol
MCP clientThe part of the host that “speaks the protocol”.AgentMCP / tool protocol
MCP serverThe “socket” provided by the tool provider, exposing capabilities like calendars, weather and files via the protocol.AgentMCP / tool protocol
GuardrailsPuts gates on the agent’s “hands and feet”: least privilege, confirmation for write actions, defence against prompt injection.AgentAgent app layer
Prompt injection“Instructions to the AI” hidden in web pages, emails or documents that try to hijack the agent.AgentGuardrails
Least privilege and human confirmationGrant only the minimum permissions the task needs, and have a person approve important actions.AgentGuardrails
EvaluationHow to tell whether an agent is good: look at completion rate, cost, speed and safety together.AgentAgent app layer
App overview › Agent › LLM
Input textThe opening you give the model, e.g. “Today the weather is really”.LLMLLM (large language model)
TokenizerCuts text into small pieces (tokens) and replaces each piece with an ID.LLMLLM (large language model)
Embedding tableLooks up a list of numbers (a vector) by ID, representing the word’s “meaning”.LLMLLM (large language model)
Position infoTells the model where each word sits in the order.LLMLLM (large language model)
N Transformer blocksProcesses each word’s vector over and over so it “understands the context” better and better.LLMLLM (large language model)
SamplingDraws one word by probability and appends it to the end of the input.LLMLLM (large language model)
Context windowThe maximum number of tokens the model can “see” at once.LLMLLM (large language model)
App overview › Agent › LLM › Neural Network Basics
NeuronThe smallest part: multiply each input by a weight, add them up, add a bias, then pass the sum through a “switch” (the activation function).Neural Network BasicsA layer (fully connected)
A layer (fully connected)Many neurons side by side, all looking at the same inputs, each giving one number.Neural Network BasicsNeural network
Neural networkMany layers stacked: each layer’s output is the next layer’s input.Neural Network BasicsLLM (large language model)
Forward passRun the input through every layer to the output, giving the model’s answer (prediction).Neural Network BasicsNeural network
Loss functionOne number measuring “how far the model’s answer is from the right answer”. Smaller is better.Neural Network BasicsBackpropagation + gradient descent
BackpropWalk back from the loss and use the chain rule to get every parameter’s gradient: “if it changes a little, how much does the loss change”.Neural Network BasicsBackpropagation + gradient descent
Update (gradient descent)Every parameter takes a small step against its gradient: new = old − learning rate × gradient.Neural Network BasicsBackpropagation + gradient descent
ActivationThe “switch” or “bend” after the weighted sum: turns straight lines into kinks and curves.Neural Network BasicsNeuron
Computation graph & chain ruleBreak the computation into small nodes joined in a graph; to differentiate, walk the graph backwards multiplying each local derivative.Neural Network BasicsBackprop
Optimizers: SGD / momentum / AdamThe rule for “exactly how to step once you have the gradient”.Neural Network BasicsUpdate (gradient descent)
Learning rateHow big each step is. One of the most important hyperparameters.Neural Network BasicsOptimizers: SGD / momentum / Adam
Mini-batches & epochsEach update uses only a small batch of examples; one pass over all the data is an epoch.Neural Network BasicsUpdate (gradient descent)
Train / validation / test setsSplit data three ways: one to learn from, one to tune settings and decide when to stop, one kept for a single final exam.Neural Network BasicsRegularization
InitializationThe small random numbers given to every weight before training starts.Neural Network BasicsNeural network
Normalization (basics)Pull a layer’s numbers back to a standard size so they don’t keep growing or shrinking.Neural Network BasicsNormalization
RegularizationWays to discourage rote memorization: L2 weight decay, dropout, early stopping, more data.Neural Network BasicsUpdate (gradient descent)
DropoutDuring training, randomly switch off part of the neurons (say half) at every step; at use time all are on.Neural Network BasicsRegularization
Convolutional network (CNN)Slide one small “filter” (kernel) across the image to find patterns, combining layer by layer: edges → textures → parts → objects.Neural Network BasicsNeural network
Recurrent neural network (RNN)Reads one word at a time, updating a “memory” (hidden state) after each, then carries it to the next word.Neural Network BasicsNeural network
LSTMAn RNN with “gates”: switches decide what to keep in memory, what to forget and what to output.Neural Network BasicsRecurrent neural network (RNN)
Word vectorsEach word gets a list of numbers (a vector); words with similar meanings get nearby vectors.Neural Network BasicsEmbedding table
App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block
AttentionWords “take a look” at each other and exchange information.Transformer blockN Transformer blocks
Residual + normKeeps the original information (residual), then brings the numbers to a stable scale (normalization).Transformer blockN Transformer blocks
Feed-forward networkEach word “digests and thinks” on its own, drawing on learned knowledge.Transformer blockN Transformer blocks
Residual connectionAdds the step’s result to the original vector instead of replacing it.Transformer blockResidual + norm
NormalizationBrings a list of numbers to a common scale.Transformer blockResidual + norm
App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › Attention
Incoming word vectorsOne vector per word (from the previous layer, or from embedding + position).AttentionAttention
Q table (makes query cards)Turns a word vector into a “query card”: what kind of word am I looking for?AttentionAttention
K table (makes key cards)Turns a word vector into a “key card”: what kind of word I am, for others to match against.AttentionAttention
V table (makes value cards)Turns a word vector into a “value card”: the information I hand over when others attend to me.AttentionAttention
Q query card (computed)Each word’s question: what am I looking for?AttentionQ table (makes query cards)
K key card (computed)Each word’s label: what am I?AttentionK table (makes key cards)
V value card (computed)The information each word can provide.AttentionV table (makes value cards)
① ScoreMatch query cards against key cards to compute match scores.AttentionAttention
② Mask (look back only)Only itself and earlier words may be seen; no peeking at later ones.AttentionAttention
③ softmax weightsTurns match scores into attention weights that add up to 100%.AttentionAttention
④ Weighted mixMixes everyone’s value cards into one new card according to the attention weights.AttentionAttention
⑤ Concat headsSeveral attention groups run at once and their results are joined end to end.AttentionAttention
⑥ Output tableMerges the concatenated multi-head results and brings them back to the original length.AttentionAttention
App overview › Agent › LLM › Transformer block › FFN & output
Output layerTurns the final vector into “one score for every word in the vocabulary”.FFN & outputLLM (large language model)
Scores (logits)One raw score per candidate word, positive or negative, not yet a probability.FFN & outputOutput layer
softmax: next-word probabilitiesTurns scores into probabilities that add up to 100%.FFN & outputLLM (large language model)
Big table 1 (expand)Expands the vector into a longer list (typically about 4× as long).FFN & outputFeed-forward network
Filter switch (activation function)Decides which detectors are “on” and which are “off”.FFN & outputFeed-forward network
Big table 2 (compress)Gathers the active features and compresses them back to the original length.FFN & outputFeed-forward network
App overview › Agent › LLM › MoE & efficiency
MoE (mixture-of-experts) layerReplaces one big feed-forward network with many “small experts”, sending each token to only a few of them.MoE & efficiencyFeed-forward network
Router / gateScores each expert and decides who gets this token.MoE & efficiencyMoE (mixture-of-experts) layer
ExpertAn independent small feed-forward network (expand – switch – compress).MoE & efficiencyMoE (mixture-of-experts) layer
Top-k selectionKeeps only the k highest-scoring experts and skips the rest entirely.MoE & efficiencyMoE (mixture-of-experts) layer
Load-balancing lossAn extra training “penalty”: if tokens crowd onto a few experts, it’s penalized.MoE & efficiencyMoE (mixture-of-experts) layer
Sparse activation: saves compute, not memoryEach token only computes a few experts, but all experts have to stand by in GPU memory.MoE & efficiencyMoE (mixture-of-experts) layer
Multi-head attention (MHA)Every head has its own Q, K and V.MoE & efficiencyAttention
Grouped-query attention (GQA / MQA)Several Q heads share one set of K and V, shrinking the KV cache several-fold.MoE & efficiencyAttention

🔤 Symbols in this card’s text

  • Say: “f”a function: a “machine” that takes in and gives back numbers (the outer one in the chain-rule row)
  • Say: “… of …”What comes out when you put the thing in brackets into the “machine” (function) named in front. Like a vending machine: put something in, get something out.
  • Say: “x”limit, chain-rule and Jacobian rows: the input number; expectation row: one result X could be; residual rows: the numbers going into the layer
  • Say: “a”limit row: the number x gets close to; dot-product row: a vector (a list of numbers); determinant row: the top-left number of the 2×2 table
  • Say: “composed with” (little circle)“Two machines joined up”: first the one on the right, then its result goes into the one on the left.
  • Say: “g”chain-rule row: the inner function (the machine that runs first)
  • Say: “prime”The little mark means “derivative”: how fast the function is changing at this point, like how steep a slope is.
  • Say: no word: side by side means timesTwo things written right next to each other, with no sign between them, are multiplied: a number right before a letter means that number times it; two brackets side by side are multiplied.
  • Say: “nabla” or “del”: the gradientThe “gradient”: how fast things change in each input direction, put in a list. It points the steepest way uphill; training takes a small step the opposite way so the loss goes down.
  • Say: “dot” (times)Another way to write times: 2·3 = 6. Between two lists of numbers (vectors) it is the “dot product”: multiply matching entries, then add them all up.
  • Say: “b”dot-product row: another vector; determinant row: the top-right number of the table
  • Say: “sigma” (sum)“Add up a whole list.” Below: where to start; above: where to stop. With only a letter below, add over every possible value of it.
  • Say: “i”a counter: which one (the row in a matrix, the word in softmax)
  • Say: “sub” (the small lowered mark)A small lowered mark is a number or a label that tells apart several things of the same kind: label 1 and label 2 are the 1st one and the 2nd one.
  • Say: “A”matrix rows: a table of numbers; Bayes row: an event we care about
  • Say: “B”matrix-product row: another table of numbers; Bayes row: the evidence we see
  • Say: “j”a counter: which one (the column in a matrix; in softmax, add up over every word j)
  • Say: “k”matrix-product row: a counter, multiply item k with item k and add them all up; the k in dₖ stands for key (the key card)
  • Say: “absolute value”Drop the plus or minus sign and keep the size: how far from 0. |−3| = 3, |3| = 3. The absolute value of a difference is the distance between the two numbers.
  • Say: “determinant”How many times a matrix scales area. Negative means the shape was flipped over; 0 means it was squashed flat onto a line (or a point).
  • Say: “d”determinant row: the bottom-right number of the table; dₖ (the √dₖ row): how many numbers are on each key card
  • Say: “c”determinant row: the bottom-left number of the 2×2 table
  • Say: “J”Jacobian row: a table of how sensitive each output is to each input; policy-gradient row: the average reward we get
  • Say: “partial” (or “del”)The partial-derivative sign: keep every other input still, move just one a tiny bit, and see how fast the result changes.
  • Say: “y”Jacobian row: the numbers the machine gives back; p − y row: the right answer (1 for the correct word, 0 for the rest); residual row: the layer’s result
  • Say: “divided by” (slash)Another way to write division: 6/3 means 6÷3 = 2.
  • Say: “expected value”“On average, about how much?”: average every outcome, weighted by how likely it is.
  • Say: “X”a random result, such as what a dice roll shows
  • Say: “p”chances: how likely each result (or word) is, between 0 and 1, adding up to 1; in the p − y row, the model’s guessed chances
  • Say: “P”P(…): the chance of what is in the brackets
  • Say: “given”Right of the bar: what we already know. Left: what we ask about. “How likely the left side is, once we know the right side.”
  • Say: “over” (the fraction bar)The top is divided by the bottom. ½ is 1 divided by 2, which is one half.
  • Say: “z”the scores: one per candidate word, can be positive or negative
  • Say: “e” (Euler’s number)A special number, about 2.718. It makes growth and change easiest to work with, the way the circle number 3.14… is special for circles.
  • Say: “to the power” (the small raised mark)A small raised number says how many times to multiply a thing by itself: 3² = 3×3 = 9, 2³ = 2×2×2 = 8. A negative power means “flip it over”: 2⁻¹ = ½.
  • Say: “H”H(p): entropy, how hard the result is to guess; H(p, q): cross-entropy, how bad guessing p with q is
  • Say: “log”“What power of the base gives this number?”: log₁₀ 100 = 2, because 10² = 100.
  • Say: “q”another set of chances used to guess p (the model’s guess)
  • Say: “KL”KL divergence: how far apart two sets of chances are (0 when equal)
  • Say: “against” (separates two things)The double bar separates the two distributions being compared: the “real” one on the left, the one that tries to match it on the right.
  • Say: “theta”all the model’s parameters (every knob)
  • Say: “becomes”Work out the right side, then store it on the left, replacing the old value, like rubbing out a scoreboard and writing the new score.
  • Say: “eta”the learning rate: how big each step is
  • Say: “L”the loss: one number for how bad the guesses are; smaller is better
  • Say: “square root”“Which number times itself gives this?”: √9 = 3, because 3×3 = 9.
  • Say: “F”the part this layer works out itself
  • Say: “I”the identity matrix: 1 on the diagonal, 0 elsewhere, i.e. “leave it unchanged”
  • Say: “R”the reward: how many points this output scored
  • Say: “pi”the policy: the model itself, giving every possible output a chance (not the circle number here)
  • Say: “tau”one complete output of the model (a string of words or actions)
